_note: The air war as its own game (the grand campaign only). Aircraft fly from airfields: places on the map with a size, which engineers can lay out and the treasury can enlarge. Each air fleet history lists is split into air groups of one kind, fighters or bombers, of at most groups.most aircraft. A group patrols, rests, or flies one raid a month. A raid is planned from its target: who can reach it, what will meet it, the chance of success and the losses to expect, and it is flown the moment the order is given.

count._note: The defences of a target as the raid card counts them (Brian, 20 November 2026: 'calculate how many flak guns they have and fighter squadrons they have that will be in range to intercept them'). The forecast has always weighed both; these put them in numbers a player can read. squadron: how many fighters make a squadron in each nation's air force ('_default' for the rest), so the fighters able to meet a raid are told in squadrons; 'later' is the larger squadron some air forces went to, as [the year it begins, its size]. guns: a target with no guns built puts up 'base' light flak guns, and each level of anti-aircraft guns built there is 'heavy' heavy guns and 'light' light ones. The historian's check (historian/raid-card-defence-count.md): a level's 120 heavy guns is 20 to 30 batteries, fair for a mid-sized target, and the record had two or three light guns to every heavy one; a British squadron was 16, a German Staffel 12 and 16 from 1944, an American squadron about 16 in 1942-43 and 25 from 1944, a Japanese chutai 9. A count only: the losses come from the same shares as before.

fields._note: sizes is how many aircraft a seeded airfield serves, by its class: 1 a landing ground, 2 an airfield, 3 an air base. Every level built on top (the arsenal's airfields, or engineers as far as 'engineers') serves arsenal.works.field.holds more. seed says where the war begins with airfields: an air base wherever history bases an air fleet and at every capital, an airfield in every city, a landing ground in every town. least is what a group stranded on bare ground can still fly. words name an airfield from the aircraft it serves.

groups._note: most is the largest group a fleet is split into. A command small enough to be one group keeps its own name. Every other group takes, once, the name of the rung of its country's ladder nearest its full strength (ruling 220, air-names.json); names._default is the plain form where no rung is near or the country has no ladder: {n} is the number and {nth} the ordinal.

raids._note: The kinds of raid the planner offers, in the order shown. needs says which aircraft can fly it at all.

kinds.label: Bomb factories and railways
kinds.blurb: Bombers go for the factories and rail yards of one province by day. Fighters in range can go with them.

kinds.label: Bomb by night
kinds.blurb: Bombers go in darkness with no escort: few are lost, and only about a third of the bombs find the target.

kinds.label: Raid troops
kinds.blurb: Fighters and bombers go for an enemy army where it stands: its organisation is cut for the battle that follows, and some of its men and guns are lost.

kinds.label: Bomb the line
kinds.blurb: Bombers go for the fieldworks of an enemy army that is dug in: months of digging are taken off its works before your army attacks. The troops dig them back a month at a time, so follow the raid with the army.

kinds.label: Bomb a town
kinds.blurb: Bombers go for the defences of a town your army stands round or beside: part of its works are broken down for the assault, and the troops inside are shaken. A town left alone mends its works month by month, so follow the raid with the army.

kinds.label: Fight for the sky
kinds.blurb: Fighters sweep the sky over one province and bombers hit its airfields. Win it and your armies and fleets have the air there for a month.

kinds.label: Strike shipping
kinds.blurb: Bombers hunt warships and merchant ships in one sea.

kinds.label: Strike a fleet
kinds.blurb: Bombers go for one enemy fleet at sea that your side has found. Carrier aircraft are trained for it; land bombers mostly are not. Its carrier fighters and its guns defend it.

kinds.label: Raid a harbour
kinds.blurb: Bombers go for the warships lying in one harbour. Ships at anchor cannot manoeuvre, and a harbour raided in the month war is declared is caught unready.

kinds.label: Bomb an airfield
kinds.blurb: Bombers go for the runways, hangars and fuel of one enemy airfield by day, with fighters in range as escort. Enough bombs shut it until its owner repairs it, aircraft parked there are destroyed, and the fighters based there go up to meet you first. (Only with airfields as targets.)

kinds.label: Scout from the air
kinds.blurb: A few aircraft photograph one province and the ground round it: every army there is seen whole until the month ends.

line._note: Bombing the line (Version 64). The works of every enemy corps dug in at the target lose bombers-that-got-through / scale months of digging, to the nearest tenth and never more than most, whatever the ground. The men are not hurt and dig as usual that month. intensity is how hard the month's flying is beside a fight for the sky (1). value is what a month off the works of one division counts for when the raid is judged. With the scale at 300 it takes 600 bombers through to take the full two months and two air groups take a little over one, so a raid and a probe together wear a finished line down without wiping it out in one month. No computer air staff flies it yet.

ground._note: A raid on troops: a month's raiding on the troops in one province. intensity is how hard the month's fighting is beside a fight for the sky (1). fighters is what one fighter is worth beside a bomber against troops. The organisation cut is weight / (scale + perDiv x enemy divisions there), never more than max, the weight being the bombers that get through and the fighters at 'fighters', times the nation's weight row where it has one (airwar.json 'weight'); troops in cover (by terrain) or dug in lose less. str is the share of the cut also lost in men and guns. Priced by the record (ruling 227, b424 and b428; historian/air-on-armies-b422.md): a month of raids on one army in 1942 and 1943 cost it 0.1 to 0.3% of its strength, in 1941 up to about 1%, and an army falling back under a sky the enemy holds 1 to 2%. The organisation cut is twice the share of men lost, about the same fighting power for a month: organisation is the game's stand-in for what air did to movement and supply. Fitted on the raids the computer flew in twelve free wars: a German raid of the usual weight (240) on 12 divisions in the open costs them 0.3%, a Soviet one 0.1 to 0.15%, and 600 bombers with 1,000 fighters on 4 divisions under a clear sky 1.8%; never more than 2%. Close support inside a battle is counted on the battle card, not here. fire is the share of the attacking fighters brought down by ground fire. value is what a point of the cut on one division counts for when the raid is judged. Set at 1,500 (ruling 227, b435, b457, b459) so that the computer's staffs fly raids on troops about as often as before the record priced them: in the free wars Germany about 34 a war on the Soviet armies, the Soviets about 11; what a raid does is not changed by it, and the card's chance and what happens are booked on the same value. At 60 no staff flew one.
ground._reach: Read only with the strafers' rule on (src/campaign/strafers.ts; the design director, 25 November 2026 05:12Z: the card, the settled raid and the fought raid charge the ground fire only on the fighters expected to be left after the air fight that have the reach to strafe). reach (G, flagged; one figure for every nation): a fighter group has the reach to go down on the troops when they lie within this share of its fighter range (air.json ftrRange and the dated range rows below, read by air.ts reach()), an escort radius that already holds about 15 to 20 minutes of fighting at the far end; a group farther out escorts its bombers and turns for home, adds no weight on the troops and is not shot at by the ground. The design director, 25 November 2026 13:35Z (historian/strafing-reach-1125.md): 0.9, because the cause is fuel: the strafers here are fighters carrying no bombs, and the record's strafers spent about 15 to 20 minutes low, flak cutting their passes short more than fuel did; the historian's sum gives 0.85 to 1.0 there. Flak is priced once, as ground fire on the strafers left (fire above): the reach is not cut again for it. A fighter carrying bombs takes 0.6 (200 miles against 350 with the tank) once the game tells fighter-bombers apart by a kit row (bomb racks) on the type: not this build. (air.json range.fullAt, the share of range at which an escort is at full effect, is another figure and is not this one.)

recon._note: A reconnaissance flight. aircraft is how many of the group go. loss is the share of them lost when enemy fighters patrol the target, per unit of their cover there. ready is the readiness the group spends.

losses._note: What a raid costs in bombers, in the air war. The share lost is bombers x (the defending fighters' share of the fighting weight over the target) to the power 'power', plus what the guns bring down. The rest of that weight is the escort, counted 'escort' times over, and the bombers' own defence (day.defence, by nation and month; by night the old flat bomberDefence of air.json). An escort saves far more than its numbers. A day raid loses no more than 'day', a night raid no more than 'most'. Fitted by ruling 227 to the historian's yardsticks (historian/raid-rows-227.json, 'fit') and the ruling's set raids (tests/raids-record-227.test.ts): 280 RAF bombers on Bremen in 1939 lose 35%, 291 American heavies on Schweinfurt in October 1943 22%, the same on the Ruhr in 1944 escorted all the way by 400 fighters 6%. By night the few fighters that find the bombers take 2 to 5%. clash is how hard the fighters of the two sides fight over a raid, beside a fight for the sky (1): the escort is there to see the bombers through, not to hunt.

day._note: Ruling 227: day raids priced by the record. Dated rows from the historian (historian/raid-rows-227.json, with marks and sources): [month, value], month 1 = September 1939; a row holds from its month until the nation's next row, and a nation with none takes _default. defence: what a nation's day bombers can do for themselves, formation, guns and turrets (1.0 is the American combat box of 1943); the bombers' side of the fighting weight is bombers x defence. kill: the defending fighters the bombers' guns bring down, for each bomber the fighters bring down, x defence (about 1 per 5.5 bombers lost at 0.35, 1 per 2 at 1.0; never none where fighters met the raid; none by night). accuracy: day bombing's weight on factories and railways (1 is full weight; the bombardment of a town under siege, and night, stay as they are). range: how far a nation's fighters reach, in km as air.json's ftrRange reads, for escort and for defence alike (a fleet row with a longer ftrRange of its own keeps it; carrier aircraft keep theirs). The historian's twin-engined long-range fighters (Germany's Bf 110 and Me 410) are not used.

weight._note: Ruling 227 (b424): a nation's real weight in the air, month by month, beside the air force named in 'against' (1.0): serviceability, training, radios and tactics, from the historian's row (historian/air-on-armies-b422.md, section 3). Each of its aircraft fights in the air as that share of one of 'against' (its quality becomes the row times that nation's quality in air.json) and weighs that share in a raid on troops. [month, value], month 1 = September 1939; the first row holds before its month too (the purged command and short courses were the same in the Winter War). A nation with no row keeps its own quality and weighs in full against troops. Only in the grand campaign's air war.

sky._note: Ruling 227 (b433): what command of the air lends a land battle in the grand campaign's air war (game.ts, the battle card; historian/sky-on-land-b431.md). The air edge is the attacker's air less the defender's over their sum (-1 to 1); 'land' is added to it where the attacker's side holds the sky over the battle, and taken off where the defender's side does; the attack is then multiplied by 1 + attack x edge and the defence by 1 - defence x edge. Fitted to the historian's bands: the attacker's sky at even air numbers x1.12 on the odds, with overwhelming air x1.25 (band x1.10 to x1.25); a contested sky at even numbers nothing (band x0.95 to x1.05); the defender's sky x0.89, and x0.79 with overwhelming air (band x0.75 to x0.90). The historical campaigns keep the old figures (land 0.3, attack 0.3, defence 0.2, the attacker's sky only). 'own' (b444, b446; historian/sky-on-land-b431.md): where nobody has won the sky over a battle, a side that can bring 'own' times the other's aircraft over it (fighters within their reach, bombers within theirs, each at its nation's weight row, the Soviet row, and at one elsewhere), and at least the least a won sky needs, holds it: overwhelming air owns the sky, as Germany's did over Poland in 1939 (about 6 to 1) and France in 1940 (1.5 to 3 to 1), and not at Kursk (about 1.07 to 1). It is contested, and nobody holds it so, where the sky there has been fought for since last month and that side did not win it, and over a nation's own home ground once it has the 'radar' technology (Britain held in 1940 at about 3.6 to 1). A sky won on the ground, as on Barbarossa's first day, is the surprise rules' business, not this.

fog._note: Fog and reconnaissance on air raids (release 2; Brian, 24 November 2026: 'you should be able to bomb a german city but you dont know what your up against without doing recon. If a squadron does a recon mission it should lift the fog of war for that area for 2 turns'; the design director's ruling of 22:10Z; src/campaign/airfog.ts). Off as shipped: a war has it with the flag rfog (setRaidFog, right after startOpen), and without the flag nothing here is read and the war plays as before. 'on' is what a new grand campaign would open with (raidFogShipped); false as shipped. With it on, a side sees the air defence of an enemy province (the enemy fighters in reach of its sky, its guns, the share of the town in ruins) only while it has the province in full sight, and remembers what it last saw there with the month (intel.airSeen). The raid card and every computer staff read that knowledge, never the truth; a raid flown is fought on the truth. The forecast is a band: its low end counts only the defence known for sure (the fighter groups whose own fields are in sight now, a carrier wing whose fleet is identified, and the guns last seen, since works stand where they are built; none where never seen); its high end adds every other fighter last seen in reach of the place, all of them rising (where the place itself was never seen, the most last seen in reach of any place within its holder's fighter reach of it), and the guns last seen, or the heaviest where none were ever seen. In sight the band is one figure, the true one, and the card's own figures are always the high end's. Any target in range can always be ordered: the fog hides, it never refuses. 'months': a reconnaissance flight gives full sight of the province and the ground beside it for this many months, the month flown and the next (Brian's '2 turns': his figure, not a guess). 'forget' (G): a sighting older than this many months is thrown away, and the place is unknown again. 'stale' (G): a staff flies a new reconnaissance over a target it is about to weigh when its last sight of it is this many months old or more, or it has never seen it. 'scouts' (G): the most such flights one staff flies in a month. 'round' (G): what is remembered of the fighters is kept to the nearest this many aircraft, since nobody counts them one by one. 'reads' (G for the opportunist; the ruling for the other two): where in the band each character of staff (rivals.json) reads a forecast, 0 the low end and 1 the high: a cautious staff the high end and a bold one the middle (the ruling), an opportunist between the two (G). 'gunsUnknown': the gun level the high end counts where the side has never seen the place: the heaviest that can be built (arsenal.json works.aa has three levels), so the high end holds whatever guns are there; not a guess. 'words': the knowledge line's words for a place seen with no guns built (a level reads as the card names it, 'level 2': the UI director, 25 Nov 2026 21:22Z, case b).

success._note: The chance of success shown before a raid: a raid succeeds when it costs the enemy more than it costs you. k is how sharply the chance turns on the expected exchange. Set from 489 raids flown by four nations over six months: at 12 the raids given 10 to 25% won 15% of the time, those given 25 to 40% won 38%, and those given over 90% all won.

ai._note: The computer's air staff. escortReady is the least readiness at which a fighter group flies escort. raids is how every computer nation at war plans raids of its own, at every level: each month 'share' of its bomber groups fit to fly go out (a group is fit with 'least' bombers and readiness 'ready'), each against the best target among the 'look' most promising it can reach, and only where the forecast gives a chance of success of 'success' or better, a gain of 'worth' aircraft or more, and bomber losses of no more than 'loss'. 'rail' is what a province with a junction and no factory is worth beside one with industry. It flies up to 'sweeps' fights for the sky a month, over front where its fighters go in at 'sky' times the odds that win it; 'skyWorth' is what the sky over an army's front is worth to it, in aircraft. The harder levels replace share, least, loss and rail for a rival (difficulty.json, bombing); the easier ones cut a rival's share. 'sour' is how a staff gives up a poor trade: a raid on factories that loses 'dear' aircraft or more and is worth less than 'trade' for each one lost, 'times' running on the same target, is not flown there again for 'rest' months (a wrecked factory or a cut railway makes it a good month). 'beach' is for a player who has named a crossing as their plan and handed the air war to the staff: it brings fighter groups up to airfields within reach of the beach, up to 'monthly' a month, until 'groups' are in reach, leaves at least 'home' guarding the homeland, and puts none on an airfield that is already full; and it sends every fit fighter group in reach up together to fight for the sky over the beach in any month it expects to win it, at 'sky' times the odds that win a sky (a staff's own offensives keep the wider margin above). A computer nation's own staff does not use it.

basing._note: Ruling 227 (b428): each month a staff bases its fighter groups by the threat (air.ts baseByThreat): every place where the nation has troops, or its own cities and works, asks for a share of its fighters as large as its share of the enemy aircraft that can reach it (fighters and bombers against troops, bombers against cities; each enemy group counted once at its real weight, airwar.json 'weight', shared among the places it reaches). A group moves to the airfield where it meets most of what is still asked for, only when that is more than 'better' times what it meets where it is, plus 'least' of its own fighters. Ruling 52(a): every stretch of front asks for a standing share besides, by the divisions the nation has there, whether or not enemy aircraft can reach it: 'presence' of all that the threat asks for, and every fighter where nothing threatens at all. So a staff with no enemy air force over it still brings its fighters up behind its army. And where a stretch of its front has stood beyond the reach of every airfield its fighters could use for 'fields' months running, a computer staff orders an airfield from the arsenal behind it (arsenal.ts aiAirfields), at a player's price and one at a time; a front that begins a new war out of reach is not waited on. And a group that can reach ground an enemy holds from where it stands moves only to a field from which it still can. A group out of the fight whose best field lies beyond a month's flight (air.json 'ferry') goes there by stages, each month to the open field within a month's flight that lies nearest to it. And with 'idle', a group left where nothing within its reach asks for fighters at all (a campaign that is over, a front that has moved on) goes to the open field within a month's flight from which it would serve the most of what is asked, though others cover it already: no group stands idle while there is work anywhere it can fly to.

ai._back: The computer's air forces fight back (Brian, 24 November 2026: "im attacking other nations that have airforces but they arent using them"; release 1.5.1). One rule for every staff (the design director, 18:38Z): with 'on', every nation's air staff in the grand campaign (the player's too while he leaves it the air war; he has each tool by hand): puts up to 'close' of its land fighters (by aircraft) on ground support over the battles it is defending, where the enemy attacked its side since last month and beside them, as well as over its own offensive's (air.json close.ai is not read while this is on); fights for the sky over a stretch of front where the armies fought since last month, not only where it is attacking, up to 'sweeps' a month at 'sky' times the odds that win one; flies 'more' times as many raids, at 'risk' more bomber losses, where the forecast gives 'success' or better and a gain of 'worth' aircraft or more (in proportion below 'full' bombers, so a small air force flies too; the enemy's troops on its own soil count 'home' times, and it never bombs its own country's factories the enemy has taken), each level keeping its own margin (difficulty.json); and the places the enemy raided since last month ask its fighters for 'raided' times the aircraft he sent there, so they go where the raids are coming. A bomber group of 'least' bombers or more may raid (small air forces have small groups), and a country fighting on its own soil (the enemy holds ground it owns, or attacked it there since last month) takes 'invaded' times the risk: it throws in what it has. 'minor': a country at war whose air force was only its air rating (nations.json 'air'; the great powers' come from air.json fleets) raises one once, with its capital held, in its first month at war: 'per' aircraft a point of its rating (at least 'least' points), 'ftr' of them fighters and the rest bombers (all fighters below 'split'), at its capital, and builds 'refit' of them a month to replace losses (air.ts raiseAirForce). Once a country has raised its groups its air rating no longer tilts its land battles (air.ts ratedAir): its air is its groups, never both. Grades (the design director, 18:38Z): close, sweeps, sky, more, risk, invaded, success, worth, full, home, least and raided are the staffs' doctrine (G), not outcome knobs; minor.per, minor.ftr and minor.refit are G/D for release 1.5.1, and release 2 replaces them with each minor's own air force at the history start, from the record. Off, every staff is as it was in release 1.5 and no country raises an air force.
